EN.1.title: Climate Change & GHG Emissions
about: This indicator looks at how much the agri-food sector contributes to climate change and what it is doing about it. It covers three things: absolute emissions from farming and food processing, emissions relative to output, and carbon stored in agricultural soils. It also tracks mitigation, such as renewable fuel production. The indicator links the sector to Canada's Paris Agreement and 2050 net-zero commitments. It focuses on sector-wide results rather than individual producers or companies, and it does not cover adaptation to climate change or indirect (scope 3) emissions across the full value chain.
observations: Farm emissions have been flat for years, but each dollar of output now carries less of them. Direct emissions from farming, including on-farm fuel use, were 69.75 Mt CO2e in 2024. That is 1.0% above 2023 and 0.8% above 2018, and the figure has hardly moved since 2017 (Figure EN.1.1.1). It is still about 37% higher than in 1990. Because Canada's total emissions have come down while farm emissions have not, agriculture now makes up 10.3% of the national total, up from 8.5% in 2010 (EN.1.1.3).

Methane and nitrous oxide account for almost all of it. Of the 56.4 Mt CO2e counted by gas in 2024 (which leaves out on-farm fuel), methane was 31.2 Mt, nitrous oxide 21.8 Mt and carbon dioxide 3.4 Mt (EN.1.1.4). Methane, nearly all of it from livestock, is about 12% below its 2000 peak. Nitrous oxide is up about 63% since 1990, and most of that comes from crop production, where it roughly doubled from 8.1 to 16.0 Mt. That is the source the 4R practices in Crop Inputs are meant to reduce. Carbon dioxide is small but has almost tripled since 1990.

Per dollar of output, farming has become considerably cleaner. Gross emissions intensity fell from 2.71 kg CO2e per dollar of primary agriculture GDP in 2010 to 1.98 in 2024, a drop of 26.7% (EN.1.1.7). Emissions rose about 14% over those years, so the gain comes from output growing faster than emissions, not from emitting less. Food processing looks different. Its intensity is about a tenth of the farm figure and has not improved, at 0.175 kg per dollar in 2010 and 0.180 in 2023, after peaking at 0.205 in 2013. In pesticide, fertilizer and other agricultural chemical manufacturing it rose from 3.35 to 4.17 over the same years.

The picture is less clear once cropland carbon is counted. The cropland sink swings so widely from year to year that it moves net emissions by tens of megatonnes (EN.1.2.1). Cropland was a 34 Mt sink in 2009, a 24 Mt source in 2022, and a 3.6 Mt sink again in 2024. The 2022 swing pushed net direct emissions to 93.9 Mt, and they were down to 48.1 Mt a year later (EN.1.1.1). Growing-season weather explains most of this, including the 2021 drought on the Prairies, so no single year says much about changes in farm practices.

Food and beverage processing adds its own emissions on top of the farm figure. Direct emissions were 6.47 million tonnes in 2023, up 23.5% from 5.24 million in 2010 (EN.1.1.2). Miscellaneous food manufacturing is the largest source at 2.2 million tonnes, followed by meat processing at 1.2 million. Animal food manufacturing grew fastest, from 0.25 to 0.46 million tonnes, while seafood processing fell by more than a third.

Emissions per unit of product are only available as single-year snapshots so far: 10.4 kg CO2e per kg of beef (live weight) and 0.97 kg per kg of milk in 2021, and 2.20 kg per kg of chicken (live weight) in 2023 (EN.1.1.5). With one year for each product, these can't show a trend yet.
Renewable fuel production is up 37.0% between 2020 and 2025 (EN.1.3.1). Output of the co-products from those plants was flat at about 1.4 to 1.5 million tonnes over the same years.

Longer-term soil carbon measures are steadier than the yearly sequestration numbers. Cumulative organic carbon has risen almost every year since the 1980s and reached 3,254 kg/ha in 2021, while tillage erosion risk fell 63.5% as conservation tillage spread (see Soil Health). The carbon building up in soils is real, even though the yearly flux bounces around with the weather.
limitations: Carbon accounting is incomplete. National Inventory Report sequestration estimates leave out enteric-methane forage offsets and on-farm tree and shrub carbon (carbon stored in maple sugarbushes alone may exceed 100 Mt CO2e). It is also worth to point out that agricultural carbon sequestration is not directly measured, that carbon stocks are not counted, and that biogenic carbon is not fully captured. What we show for cropland (EN.1.2.1) rests on inventory estimates.

Some of the inventory's accounting choices affect how emissions are split. It groups perennial forage and silage crops with livestock rather than crops, which may shift emissions between the crop and animal figures in EN.1.1.4. Calculation rules also differ across sectors, so comparing farm and processing emissions needs care, and where proxy data is used there is little sector detail. On-farm fuel use is still lumped in with fisheries in the national accounts.

The data do not yet cover everything the indicator is meant to show. There is nothing on the adoption of mitigation practices, on-farm renewable energy use, or progress against national reduction targets. Renewable fuel production (EN.1.3.1) is the only mitigation measure, and it measures production rather than use in the sector.

Coverage is thinner in places. The processing-sector series stops at 2023, and its emissions per dollar of GDP covers 10 of the 11 sub-sectors because GDP is not published for tobacco on its own. Emissions intensity for animal products is only available as single-year snapshots (beef and milk in 2021, chicken in 2023). The Centre’s partners also note that the definitions for measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) still need development.
opportunities: Add measures for the parts of the indicator's purpose the data cannot yet show: adoption of mitigation practices, on-farm renewable energy use, and progress against national reduction targets.
Work with partners on MRV definitions and on how forage, silage and carbon stocks are counted, so the sequestration picture is more complete

EN.2.title: Soil Health
observations: Soil cover reached 276.1 days a year in 2021, up 8.2% from 1971. All of that gain came after 1981, when cover was still about 255 days, the same as in 1971 (EN.2.1.1).

Erosion risk has dropped a lot. Overall risk fell 57.4% between 1981 and 2021, from 12.75 to 5.43 (EN.2.2.1). Tillage was the biggest piece, falling 63.5% (7.96 to 2.90) as conservation and no-till practices spread. Wind erosion fell from 3.75 to 1.22, and water erosion improved least, from 3.83 to 2.75. Nearly all of this progress came before 2011, when overall risk was already 5.63. Since then water erosion has crept back up, from 2.59 to 2.75.

Soil organic carbon has kept building. Cumulative carbon gain reached 3,254 kg/ha by 2021 (EN.2.3.2), and the relative organic carbon index rose from 0.763 to 0.791 (EN.2.3.4), gaining a little more in the last decade than in the one before. The yearly gain has grown from about 9 kg/ha in the 1980s to about 125 kg/ha since 2011, although it swings a lot from one year to the next, from 77 to 236 kg/ha in the 2010s (EN.2.3.1). The risk of organic carbon degradation dropped from 2.47 in 1981 to 1.56 by 1991 and has stayed near 1.5 since, on a scale where 1 is very low and 4 is high (EN.2.3.3).

These long-run trends give context for Climate Change. Soil carbon builds up over decades, while cropland sequestration in any one year depends on the weather, so the two don't move together from year to year.

Farmland conversion is only tracked for Alberta so far (EN.2.4.1). Between 2011 and 2025 the province lost about 82,600 ha of prime agricultural land (Classes 1 to 3), or 0.7% of the 12.3 million ha it started with. Marginal land (Class 4) held steady at 4.08 million ha, and non-arable pasture (Classes 5 to 7) grew slightly, by about 18,400 ha. The pace of loss has eased, from about 7,600 ha a year between 2019 and 2022 to about 3,800 ha a year between 2022 and 2025.
limitations: The indicator is meant to cover physical, chemical and biological properties (Indicator Scope Consensus), but the data mostly capture the first two: soil cover, erosion and organic carbon. The 2025 National Index notes that compaction, biological diversity, drainage capacity, pH and salinity are missing, and there is no composite soil health index. Practice measures such as crop rotation are not included either.

Soil biology is the biggest gap. Partners say datasets in places like Ontario and Atlantic Canada are one-off measurements, and open data for tests such as POXC (active carbon) is privately owned and hard to get even though the testing is widespread.

Without a consolidated national dataset, access to provincial data varies a lot. Nothing was found for Saskatchewan. Quebec datasets are not publicly available and covered by non-disclosure agreements with producers. Data from Atlantic Canada has to be stripped of identifying information before release, and Alberta's lab data is not centralized, so each private lab would need to be approached.

The national soil series all stop at 2021, because AAFC updates its soil indicators on a multi-year cycle. Water erosion is also calculated differently across regions (Manitoba uses a 0 to 100 index, Atlantic Canada other standard methods), which makes regional comparisons shaky.

Farmland conversion is only tracked well in Alberta, which has 14 years of detailed reports (EN.2.4.1 here covers 2011 to 2025). National Inventory Report data on conversion to permanent settlements is outdated, and Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Quebec have nothing comparable.

Residual nitrogen, which would link soil management to water quality, is not in the data. Partners note that the depth measured matters (0 to 60 cm versus 30 to 60 cm) and that it flags risk rather than measuring the soil's capacity to protect water.
opportunities: Build a composite soil health index that brings physical, chemical and biological measures together, and add practice measures such as crop rotation and residual nitrogen.
Agree data-sharing arrangements with provinces (Quebec, Atlantic Canada, Alberta labs) and an open, standard set of soil biology tests such as POXC, to start building trend data.
Extend land conversion beyond Alberta, using Alberta's reporting as the template, and agree a common water erosion method across regions.

EN.3.title: Water Stewardship
about: This indicator looks at how the agri-food sector uses water and how it affects water quality. It has two parts. Quality covers the condition of freshwater influenced by agriculture, including pesticide detections. Use covers the volume of water drawn for crop production, livestock and food processing. It reflects growing climate variability and rising expectations for responsible resource use. It does not measure water stress directly, climate adaptation outcomes or consumer water use.
observations: Crop irrigation volumes peaked at 2.95 billion m³ in 2018, fell 39.7% to 1.78 billion m³ in 2020, rose to 2.09 billion in 2022 and came back to 1.89 billion in 2024 (EN.3.2.1, EN.3.2.5). The swings follow rainfall in Alberta, where most of Canada's irrigated land is. Volumes were higher in the dry years (2018, 2022) and lower in the wet ones (2020, 2024). Changes in irrigated area and crop mix play a part too.

Irrigated area has gone the other way, growing from 605,907 ha in 2020 to 769,117 ha in 2024, up 27.0% (EN.3.2.4). Volume rose only 6% over the same years, so the water applied per hectare fell about 17%, from roughly 2,940 m³ to 2,450 m³. Per hectare, 2018 stands out at about 4,270 m³. Better irrigation efficiency could be part of the reason, but weather and crop mix matter too, and tracking water use per hectare over time would give a clearer read.

Crop and animal production both used more water between 2019 and 2021, up 30.9% for crops and 21.1% for livestock (EN.3.2.2). Going back to 2009, livestock water use is up 43% and crop use up 64%, though the series is only reported every second year. 2021 was a drought year on the Prairies, which probably explains some of the recent jump.

Processors went the other way. Water intake by food and beverage manufacturers dropped 19.4%, from 406.1 million m³ in 2013 to 327.1 million m³ in 2021 (EN.3.2.3). All of the drop was in food manufacturing (367.0 down to 283.4 million m³, or 22.8%), while beverage and tobacco intake rose from 39.1 to 43.7 million m³. Without production data we can't say whether this reflects better efficiency or simply lower output.

On water quality, 45.4% of monitored river sites were rated Excellent or Good in 2022 to 2024, 39.9% Fair, 13.0% Marginal and 1.7% Poor (EN.3.1.1). Pesticides turned up in 1.6% of water samples in 2024, compared with 1.9% in 2023 and 1.7% in 2022 (EN.3.1.2). Three years is too short to call a trend.
limitations: Water stress, meaning withdrawals compared with natural replenishment, is not measured at the national scale, and partners note that Environment and Climate Change Canada discontinued that metric about 10 years ago. Without it the indicator cannot show pressure on supply or regional differences.

The metrics count absolute water use for crops, livestock and processing, with no context on how much water is in the final product (about 16% moisture in grain compared with 75 to 80% in tomatoes or lettuce), so comparisons across products can mislead. Greenhouse water use and product-level water intensity are not tracked.

Water efficiency and water management practices are not measured yet, even though the indicator is meant to show how efficiently water is used. The quality series are short: the river index covers 2022 to 2024, pesticide detections start in 2022, and it is uncertain whether the pesticide monitoring pilot continues beyond its two-year run.

Several series end early or have gaps. Crop and animal production water use stops at 2021 and is reported every second year, and processing water use stops at 2021 with irregular years. Irrigation is concentrated in Alberta, so national irrigation totals mostly follow prairie weather.
opportunities: Calculate water productivity ($ per m³) by pairing water use with sector GDP or receipts, and adjust for water content of products so crops, livestock and processing can be compared fairly.
Add greenhouse water use and product-level water intensity, and secure the continuation of pesticide-in-water monitoring. Restoring a national water stress measure would fill the biggest gap.

EN.4.title: Biodiversity & Agrobiodiversity
about: Biodiversity is hard to measure directly, so this indicator uses habitat as a stand-in. It follows the condition of, and changes to, habitats in agricultural and marine landscapes, including wildlife habitat capacity on farmland, land-cover change and fish stock harvest levels. The agrobiodiversity side asks how well working farmland supports pollination, pest control and resilient food production. The aim is to show whether ecosystems are being conserved, restored or lost. It does not yet capture species-level trends or genetic diversity.
observations: Wildlife habitat capacity on agricultural land fell 3.0% between 2000 and 2020, from 30.75 to 29.81 (EN.4.1.1). About 80% of the loss came between 2005 and 2015, when the index dropped by roughly 0.07 to 0.08 points a year. From 2015 to 2020 it slowed to under 0.01 points a year (EN.4.1.2). That could mean the decline is levelling off, but it is only one five-year period.

Land cover changes help explain the drop. Between 2000 and 2020, native grassland and unimproved pasture, the most valuable habitat types, lost 0.42 and 0.20 percentage points of agricultural land area. Coniferous and deciduous woodland lost 1.75 and 1.25 points, and perennial cropland lost 0.92. Regenerating woodland after harvest (+2.22) and annual cropland (+1.29) gained the most, and built-up land (settlement, vegetated settlement and roads) grew by 0.72 (EN.4.3.1).

Fisheries look better than they did a decade ago. In 2024, 96.5% of key fish stocks (191 of 198) were harvested at or below removal references or other approved levels, up from 89.7% in 2011 (EN.4.1.3). Most of the gain came by 2013 though. The share has stayed between 94% and 99% every year since 2012.
limitations: Habitat is a proxy for biodiversity, and the data cannot yet show species-level trends, genetic diversity or long-term biodiversity tracking. The index behind wildlife habitat capacity focuses mainly on vertebrates, which leaves pollinators and other invertebrates out.
Conversion of farmland and grassland is not available nationally. It is only tracked for Alberta (EN.2.4.1), and the 2025 National Index flags missing farmland-to-urbanization conversion data.
There is no measure of crop diversity or landscape heterogeneity (field size, buffers, habitat features), and no composite or disaggregated biodiversity view.
The data are dated and coarse. Habitat capacity is reported in five-year steps to 2020, land-cover change covers 2000 to 2020, and the fish stock measure describes fisheries rather than farmland.
opportunities: Build an adapter for the national Loss of Farmland report (National Inventory Report 6.8.2.1.1), which is already collected, and extend provincial conversion data beyond Alberta.
Add measures of crop diversity, landscape heterogeneity, and pollinators and other invertebrates, and combine them into a composite biodiversity view.

EN.5.title: Crop Input Use & Management
about: This indicator looks at how fertilizers, pesticides and other crop inputs are used and how well they are managed. It covers how much is used and whether farmers adopt practices that cut losses to soil, water and air, such as 4R nutrient stewardship, variable rate application and soil testing. The aim is to keep yields up while reducing runoff, emissions and other pressure on ecosystems. Because environmental outcomes are hard to measure at scale, it leans on proxy measures and practice adoption.
observations: 4R Nutrient Stewardship adoption is now reported by crop and region, and most categories gained ground between 2024 and 2025 (EN.5.2.1). Corn in Ontario almost doubled, from 7.8% to 14.5% of sampled hectares. Canola in Western Canada rose from 26.2% to 35.3%, spring wheat in Western Canada from 29.9% to 36.9%, and feed barley in Manitoba from 33.8% to 40.9%. Malt barley in Manitoba jumped from 8.4% to 42.6%, a change big enough that it is worth double-checking before leaning on it. Grain corn in Quebec went the other way, dropping from 11.2% to 3.2%.

Variable rate technology is used on a modest share of hectares, mostly 7% to 20%, and the direction differs by region (EN.5.2.2). In the west it has crept up: canola went from 14.8% in 2019 to 19.5% in 2025, spring wheat from 12.7% in 2016 to 17.4%, and Manitoba malt barley from 10.4% to 19.4% since 2022. In the east it has slipped. Ontario corn went from 12.5% to 8.6%, Ontario winter wheat from 9.0% in 2015 to 2.1%, Quebec grain corn from 10.3% to 7.7%, and PEI potatoes from 25.6% to 16.7% since 2022.

How often farmers test their soil depends heavily on where they farm (EN.5.2.3). In Manitoba about 62% of hectares are tested for nitrogen every year, and in Western Canada about 45%, up from 30% in 2019. Ontario and PEI mostly test on a three-year cycle (36% and 71% of hectares for nitrogen), with only 3% of Ontario hectares tested every year. Quebec has the least testing, at 6% every year and 20% every three years. Testing for pH, phosphorus and potassium follows the same pattern, at 60% every year in Manitoba, 43% in Western Canada and 1.3% in Ontario.

Liquid manure was applied to about 1.18 million ha in 2021, and 58% of that (682,433 ha) was injected or incorporated into the soil. The other 499,637 ha was left on the surface, where more nitrogen tends to be lost as ammonia (EN.5.2.4). It is a single year, so there is no trend yet.

Chemical-residue compliance for fresh produce has stayed high, between 98.3% and 99.4% in each of the seven survey cycles since 2016–17 (EN.5.1.1). In the latest cycle (2022–23) there were 9 pesticide violations in 1,289 samples. Pesticide detections in water were also low, at 1.6% of samples in 2024 (see Water Stewardship). The two measures capture different things, but both sit at favourable levels.

Nutrient use efficiency moves around from year to year (EN.5.2.5). Nitrogen efficiency ranged from 62% to 81% between 2012 and 2024, with the lowest reading in the 2021 drought year and the highest in 2022, and it has stayed above 76% for the last three years. Nitrogen inputs held around 5 million tonnes a year while crop removal grew, from 3.2 million tonnes in 2012 to 4.1 million in 2024. Phosphorus efficiency ranged from 83% to 116%. It has been above 100% since 2022, which means crops removed more phosphorus than was applied and soil reserves are being drawn down.

New variety registrations are concentrated in oilseeds, at 58 to 214 a year, compared with 6 to 45 for each of the other major crop groups (EN.5.3.1). Soybean accounts for most of that, at up to 181 registrations a year, and canola adds 12 to 40. Oilseed counts peaked at 214 in 2023 and were 62 in 2025. The data don't say which traits, such as drought tolerance or disease resistance, these registrations are meant to improve. Registrations don't line up with yields in the current data (EC.5.1.1). Canola yields rose about 32% between 2010 and 2025, from 1,900 to 2,507 kg/ha, yet year-to-year registrations and canola yields show no relationship, and soybean yields were flat at about 3,000 kg/ha even though soybean has the most registrations. Weather moves yields far more than variety releases do (canola fell to 1,593 kg/ha in the 2021 drought). Seeded area is not in the current data, so we can't yet separate the effect of new varieties from changes in acreage.
limitations: Practice adoption data are short and regional. The 4R series has only two years (2024 and 2025) and six crop and region combinations across four regions, so it cannot show a trend, is not national, and a jump like Manitoba malt barley cannot be checked against earlier years. Variable rate use and soil testing cover a handful of regions and crops, and liquid manure application is a single year (2021).

The link between inputs, productivity and environmental performance is hard to see. New variety registrations do not track yields (EC.5.1.1), and seeded area is not in the current data, so the effect of new varieties cannot be separated from changes in acreage.
opportunities: Add a pesticide-use-intensity metric (use per hectare of cropland) and a measure of integrated pest management adoption.
Extend the 4R, variable rate and soil testing series across more years, crops and regions, and repeat the liquid manure survey so there is a trend.

EN.6.title: Food Loss & Waste
about: This indicator looks at how much food is lost or wasted in the agri-food system, and how losses are prevented or put to other uses. The focus is on losses before the consumer: on the farm, in storage, processing and transport, and at retail. It covers two ideas, preventing loss and diverting what is lost, for example to animal feed, compost or upcycled products. It ties into national and global targets, including halving food loss by 2030. Consumer-level waste is out of scope, and there is no standard way yet to measure loss at every stage.
observations: Within this indicator's scope (before the consumer), avoidable food loss and waste was estimated at 6.67 million tonnes in the latest report (EN.6.1.1). About two thirds of it, 4.39 million tonnes, is lost upstream in preharvest, storage and grading, and processing, with processing and manufacturing the largest single stage at 2.81 million. Distribution and retail add 2.28 million tonnes. The same source also estimates 0.67 million tonnes at restaurants, hotels and institutions and 1.48 million at households, which sit outside this indicator's scope.

Animal feed is also a big destination for Canadian grain. In 2025 the domestic feed industry used 80% of Canadian barley, 60% of corn and 30% of wheat production (EN.6.2.2). That grain doesn't go straight to people. It becomes meat, milk, eggs and other animal products, which matters when thinking about grain in the context of food availability and food security.

Oilseed crushing leaves by-products that also go to feed. Canola meal production reached 6.79 million tonnes in 2025, up 32.7% from 2017, while soybean meal held between 1.2 and 1.6 million tonnes and came in at 1.22 million in 2024, its lowest in the series (EN.6.2.3). Using the meal for livestock feed puts to work what is left after the oil is extracted. These volumes shouldn't be compared directly with the food loss estimates, because the two are counted on different bases.
limitations: Several figures have not been refreshed, and none has a confirmed update date. The Reduce estimates (4.39 million tonnes before distribution, 2.28 million at distribution and retail) come from a report that partners say relies on a 2019 baseline, while the 2025 National Index describes them as modelled on 2020 data. Two Repurpose metrics, government waste-reduction funding and non-marketable wheat used for feed, were not updated in the 2025 cycle. Partners add that the Reduce data may be a one-off, and that future updates of the Food Waste Reduction Challenge, which feeds the Repurpose sub-indicator, are uncertain.
With one snapshot (2024 in this pipeline) there is no trend, so the data cannot yet show progress toward the national and global goal of halving food loss by 2030.

Coverage is narrower than the scope. The indicator is meant to cover avoidable and unavoidable (inedible) loss, and diversion to animal feed, compost, upcycled products, biofuels and anaerobic digesters. The data have avoidable loss only, diversion only through animal feed (grain shares and oilseed meal), and nothing on prevention initiatives.

Comparisons with global data are unreliable. FAO food systems dashboard figures for cereal, pulse, vegetable and fruit loss put Canada above the world average, which partners find counterintuitive and want investigated.
opportunities: Agree an update schedule for the Reduce estimates and the Repurpose metrics, and build a baseline and time series so progress toward the 2030 target can be tracked.
Add unavoidable loss and other diversion routes (compost, anaerobic digesters, upcycled products), plus measures of prevention initiatives and of policy and funding programs.
Investigate the FAO dashboard methodology so Canada can be compared with global figures with confidence.

EN.7.title: Packaging & Waste
about: This indicator looks at how packaging and plastic waste is generated, managed and reduced across the agri-food system, using the reduce, reuse and recycle framework. It covers on-farm plastics such as pesticide containers and grain bags, as well as packaging used in processing and retail. It tracks diversion, recycling and uptake of circular practices, in support of national commitments on plastic waste. It does not yet measure reuse at scale or capture every type of packaging.
observations: Recycling of small pesticide and fertilizer containers has improved, though not in a straight line. The recycling rate was 66% in 2013, hovered around 61% to 62% from 2014 to 2017, and has climbed since 2018, reaching 88% in 2025, with a single dip in 2022 from 77% to 73% (EN.7.1.3). The weight collected rose from 1.63 kilotonnes in 2011 to 2.50 in 2025, up 54% (EN.7.1.1).

Plastics are a less positive story (EN.7.1.2). Residential plastics diversion dipped from 230,777 tonnes in 2018 to 198,756 in 2022, then recovered to 235,198 in 2024, about 1.9% above 2018. Non-residential diversion fell in every reporting period, from 97,813 tonnes in 2018 to 66,883 in 2024, a drop of 31.6%. It is the one clear step backward among the packaging and waste measures.
limitations: Cleanfarms archived its container-count metric and now reports weight in kilograms, which is what the container series here (EN.7.1.1) uses. The 2025 National Index notes no replacement was identified for the old metric, so the recycling rate (EN.7.1.3) should be checked against the same change.

Reuse is not measured. No data were found for the Reuse sub-indicator even though it was identified in 2023, and Cleanfarms only holds reuse data for a single product line. All three metrics here cover reduce and recycle only.
Composting and diversion are not tracked. Cleanfarms does not track compost diversion, and there are no active composting metrics.
Collection volumes differ by region partly because provincial extended producer responsibility (EPR) rules differ, so national totals and trends blend different rules.
Coverage is narrower than the scope. The plastics diversion series (EN.7.1.2) is not specific to agri-food, and there is no measure of the packaging generated, or of processing and retail packaging.
opportunities: Add composting and diversion metrics, packaging from processing and retail, and agri-specific plastics such as grain bags, and show collection results alongside each province's EPR rules.

FI.1.title: Safe Food
about: The Safe Food indicator assesses the performance of Canada’s food safety system, focusing on the outcomes of regulatory oversight, population health outcomes, compliance, and system response to food safety risks across the agri-food system.

The indicator measures system-level food safety safeguards that underpin trust in Canadian food and support access to domestic and international markets. It assesses the overall safety of Canada’s food system through regulatory compliance, investigations, recalls, chemical-residue monitoring and foodborne illness. New metrics have been added to provide more accurate and comprehensive information on prevention, detection and response, while recognizing that no single measure can determine whether the food supply is becoming safer.
observations: Canada continues to record high regulatory compliance. The proportion of tested imported and domestic food products meeting federal requirements increased from 97.6% in 2022–23 to 98.6% in 2024–25. The percentage of federally registered food establishments that corrected identified issues following inspection also rose from 75.4% to 85.8%, reaching the CFIA target of at least 85%.

Public confidence has also improved. The percentage of Canadians who agreed that the CFIA helps ensure food sold in Canada is safe increased from 71.5% in 2022–23 to 82% in 2024–25. This new metric responds to an opportunity identified in 2025 by providing information on public perceptions of Canada’s food-safety oversight.

Food-safety investigations increased from 2,529 in 2021–22 to 3,934 in 2025–26, while recalls rose from 196 in 2024 to 271 in 2025. These increases may reflect changes in food-safety risks, but they may also result from stronger surveillance, reporting or regulatory activity. Even though, Investigation and recall totals alone do not demonstrate that food became less safe.

The proportion of higher-risk recalls initiated before an adverse effect was reported declined from 92.1% in 2023–24 to 71.9% in 2024–25. This decline warrants attention because the measure reflects the system’s ability to identify and remove higher-risk products before illnesses or injuries are reported.

Residue monitoring results continue to demonstrate strong performance, with available compliance rates generally above 93%. In 2020–21, pesticide-residue compliance was 99.2% for domestic fresh fruits and vegetables and 93.8% for imported products.

The addition of foodborne outbreak data provides further information on safety outcomes. In 2024, PHAC coordinated investigations of 10 outbreaks involving 286 reported cases, compared with six outbreaks and 693 cases in 2023. Salmonella accounted for four outbreaks and 122 cases in 2024. Although the number of outbreaks increased, associated cases declined by approximately 59%. Annual results can be influenced by a small number of large outbreaks and should be interpreted cautiously.
limitations: Assessing Canada’s food-safety performance remains challenging because relevant results are dispersed across departmental reports, surveillance studies and recall databases that use different measures and scopes. Recall totals must also be interpreted carefully: one incident can generate numerous product recalls. Canada’s surveillance system depends on information shared among federal, provincial, territorial and regional authorities, which can affect the completeness and timeliness of national reporting. Additional limitations include inspection coverage gaps, uneven traceability across complex supply chains, risks associated with imported foods and food fraud, and limited publicly consolidated information connecting inspections, recalls, illnesses and corrective actions over time.
opportunities: Canada already has several initiatives supporting stronger food traceability. The Safe Food for Canadians Regulations require most food businesses to maintain one-step-back and one-step-forward records. CFIA also manages the national Livestock Traceability Program, has explored boat-to-plate traceability for seafood and completed a blockchain pilot for supply-chain information sharing1. Its current digital modernization agenda includes updated data and analytics strategies and improved digital-service platforms. Together, these initiatives provide a strong foundation and an opportunity to develop an interoperable, end-to-end digital traceability system that enables faster investigations, more targeted recalls and improved detection of food fraud.
notes: CFIA completed a two-year initiative examining the practical application of blockchain for information sharing, supply-chain management and traceability. https://inspection.canada.ca/en/about-cfia/acts-and-regulations/forward-regulatory-plan/targeted-regulatory-review

FI.2.title: Nutrition Information
about: The Nutrition Information indicator assesses Canada’s approach to providing transparent, standardized, and reliable nutrition information to consumers. It focuses on the availability, accessibility, and clarity of nutrition information provided through regulatory frameworks, disclosure requirements, and public guidance that support informed food choices and healthier diets at the population level. The indicator captures key areas related to nutrition labelling, front-of-package labelling, nutrition information availability, and consumer transparency . It evaluates the extent to which consumers have access to consistent and understandable nutrition information across the food system.

While the indicator aligns strongly with the Food Integrity Block through its focus on transparency and consumer access to information, it does not directly measure nutrition or health outcomes, dietary behaviours, or the overall nutritional quality of diets.

New metrics have been added to provide a more accurate and comprehensive assessment. The previous Indicator focused mainly on the existence of nutrition-labelling and fortification requirements. The expanded metrics include use of Health Canada’s dietary guidance, nutrient-content and disease-risk-reduction claims, implementation of front-of-package labelling, and food misrepresentation. These additions broaden the Indicator from documenting regulations to considering how nutrition information is communicated, used, and accurately represented.
observations: Canada’s Food Guide remains the foundation of national dietary guidance. It was last updated in 2019, replacing the 2007 version. Health Canada’s 2025 evidence review1 concluded that the current dietary guidance remains scientifically relevant, while identifying emerging evidence that may inform future updates.

Nutrition information can be mandatory, including the Nutrition Facts table, ingredient list and allergen declarations, or voluntary, including nutrient-content claims such as “source of calcium” or “low in fat.” Disease-risk-reduction claims may also be used when foods meet prescribed conditions. Permitted claims address relationships between diet and health outcomes such as hypertension, osteoporosis, heart disease, cancer, and dental caries.

The most significant regulatory change since the 2025 Index is the implementation of front-of-package nutrition labelling. As of January 1, 2026, most prepackaged foods that meet or exceed prescribed thresholds for saturated fat, sugars, or sodium must display a front-of-package “high in” symbol, subject to regulated exemptions. Products imported, manufactured in Canada, or packaged at retail before that date may continue to be sold.2 This requirement responds directly to an opportunity identified in 2025 and provides consumers with more visible information about nutrients of public-health concern.

The percentage of Canadians reported as using Health Canada’s dietary guidance was 44.3% from 2022–23 through 2024–25, below the federal target of at least 50%. However, these results rely on Canadian Community Health Survey data last made available in 2021–22 and do not represent newly measured annual values.3

Canada also requires specified foods to be fortified with particular nutrients. Examples include iodine in table salt, vitamin D in milk and margarine, and B vitamins, iron, and folic acid in white flour.

The addition of food-misrepresentation data recognizes that nutrition information must be accurate and trustworthy. In targeted 2022–23 testing, satisfactory results ranged from 62% for other expensive oils and 68% for grated hard cheese to 90% for fruit juice and 98% for meat.
limitations: Assessing nutrition information in Canada remains challenging because several measures track the existence of regulatory requirements rather than their implementation or effectiveness. Public data are limited on the number of products requiring front-of-package symbols, compliance rates, nutrient-content claims and changes in product formulation. The indicator also does not assess whether consumers understand nutrition information or whether it changes purchasing and dietary behaviour. Health Canada’s repeated 44.3% result for 2022–23 through 2024–25 relies on Canadian Community Health Survey data last available in 2021–22 and therefore cannot demonstrate annual change. The recent introduction of mandatory front-of-package labelling also means that its effects cannot yet be evaluated reliably.
opportunities: Canada’s implementation of front-of-package labelling and new supplemented-food requirements creates an important opportunity to improve both nutrition information and its measurement. These initiatives could support systematic monitoring of label compliance, consumer awareness and understanding, product reformulation and changes in purchasing behaviour. Combined with Canada’s Food Guide, consumer-education resources and ongoing monitoring of food advertising to children, they provide a foundation for assessing whether nutrition policies improve access to clear information and support healthier choices. Establishing a national baseline and publishing regular results would allow Canada to move beyond measuring the existence of requirements toward evaluating their implementation, reach and effectiveness..
notes: Health Canada, Front-of-package nutrition symbol labelling guide
Health Canada, 2024–25 Departmental Results Report, Departmental Result 5: Canadians make healthy choices, Table 6, Footnote e. Access the official report

FI.3.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship
about: The Antimicrobial Stewardship indicator assesses Canada’s approach to promoting the responsible, prudent, and sustainable use of antimicrobials across the agri-food system. It focuses on the policies, practices, monitoring systems, and stewardship measures implemented to reduce antimicrobial resistance risks while supporting animal health, food system integrity, and public health protection.

In Canada, sales of antimicrobials for farmed and domestic animals are tracked through national surveillance systems, including the Veterinary Antimicrobial Sales Reporting system and the Canadian Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System. CARSS also monitors antimicrobial use and resistance trends across human and animal health. Together, these datasets provide an evidence base for assessing stewardship progress and identifying risks to public health and the agri-food system.

Updated species-specific sales and resistance metrics provide a more accurate and comprehensive assessment than total sales alone. They also strengthen alignment with the One Health approach, which recognizes the connections among human, animal, plant, and environmental health.
observations: Total veterinary antimicrobial sales declined from 1,064.3 tonnes in 2020 to 917.17 tonnes in 2024, a reduction of approximately 13.8%. Sales in 2024 were also 6.1% lower than the 976.8 metric tonnes reported in 2023. This sustained decline is a positive development, although sales volume alone cannot determine whether antimicrobials were used appropriately or explain the factors driving the change.

Species-specific results present a mixed picture. Between 2023 and 2024, biomass-adjusted sales of medically important antimicrobials increased for pigs from 134 to 139.5 milligrams per kilogram of biomass. Sales declined for cattle from 66 to 56.5 mg/kg and for poultry from 68 to 48.1 mg/kg. These decreases suggest continued progress in some production sectors.

In contrast to the decline reported in the 2025 Index, aquaculture sales increased sharply from 58 mg/kg in 2023 to 221.9 mg/kg in 2024. This increase should be interpreted cautiously because changes in animal biomass, disease conditions, production cycles, and the timing or attribution of sales can produce substantial annual variation. Additional information is needed to determine whether the result represents a sustained change.

Antimicrobial resistance remains a significant concern. Between 2018 and 2022, CARSS identified upward trends for several priority infections, including community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, and resistant Salmonella infections. Healthcare-associated MRSA bloodstream infections, Clostridioides difficile infections, and drug-resistant tuberculosis remained stable.1

The addition of resistance trends strengthens the Indicator by recognizing that stewardship involves both responsible use and the preservation of treatment effectiveness. However, the reported resistance trends relate mainly to human infections and cannot be attributed directly to antimicrobial use in agriculture.
limitations: Current data are largely based on sales information, which provides a useful proxy but does not show how antimicrobials are administered on farms or whether they are used for treatment, disease prevention, or other purposes. Biomass adjustment improves comparison but does not fully account for production systems, disease pressure, animal lifespans, or treatment intensity.

Coverage across the One Health spectrum remains uneven. The resistance component primarily describes human infections and is not directly linked to animal-use results. Reporting periods also differ, with sales data extending to 2024 and most resistance trends ending in 2022. Environmental surveillance and nationally representative farm-level data remain limited.
opportunities: Future reporting could integrate sales data with farm-level use, prescribing purposes, animal-health outcomes, and resistance findings from animals, food, people, and environmental sources. Results could also be presented by antimicrobial class, administration route, species, production stage, and region.

Canada’s 2023–2027 Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance provides an opportunity to strengthen standardized One Health surveillance and integrate antimicrobial-use and resistance data across sectors.2 Developing linked, longitudinal datasets would support clearer assessment of stewardship progress, improve international comparability, and reinforce the credibility of Canada’s antimicrobial stewardship efforts.
notes: Public Health Agency of Canada, CARSS: 2024 Key Findings
Public Health Agency of Canada, Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance: Year 2 Progress Report

FI.4.title: Zoonotic Disease Mitigation
about: The Zoonotic Disease Mitigation indicator assesses Canada’s capacity to prevent, monitor, manage, and mitigate zoonotic disease risks across the agri-food system. It focuses on the systems, frameworks, and practices implemented to reduce the transmission of diseases between animals, humans, and the environment, while supporting food system integrity, public health protection, and animal health management.

The Indicator focuses on Risk Surveillance, including the prevention of animal-disease incursions, confirmed outbreaks detected through CFIA investigations and producer participation in animal-health protection programs. New metrics have been added to provide more accurate and comprehensive information. They broaden the Indicator beyond border biosecurity by considering disease occurrence within Canada and producer participation in preventive programs. Together, these measures provide a stronger basis for assessing preparedness and response.
observations: According to CFIA’s 2023–24 Departmental Results Report, no cases of animal diseases posing a risk to animal or human health were identified as having entered Canada. This maintains the result reported in 2020–21 and reflects regulatory controls, import requirements and surveillance for high-risk animals and animal products. However, the result does not mean that Canada experienced no animal or zoonotic diseases during the reporting period.

The addition of a domestic outbreak measure provides important context. The rate of confirmed animal-disease outbreaks declined slightly from 28 per 100 CFIA investigations in 2022–23 to 27 in 2023–24, before increasing to 37.5 in 2024–25. This result was substantially above CFIA’s target of no more than three outbreaks per 100 investigations. CFIA attributed the result to ongoing highly pathogenic avian influenza infections transmitted from wild birds to domestic poultry.¹ The increase therefore reflects a significant continuing disease event rather than a general deterioration across all animal diseases.

Producer participation provides another perspective on prevention. The percentage of participating producers who maintained or improved their status in animal-health protection programs increased from 94% in 2022–23 to 97% in 2023–24, before declining to 86% in 2024–25. CFIA reported that the decline was associated with fewer herds enrolled in voluntary programs addressing chronic wasting disease, scrapie and enzootic bovine leukosis.

Canada also has a compulsory national livestock traceability program covering cattle, bison, sheep, pigs and farmed wild boars. Managed by CFIA under the Health of Animals Act and regulations, the system uses animal identification and movement information to support disease investigations, control measures and emergency response. Its existence strengthens Canada’s capacity to identify potentially affected animals and premises and to respond more rapidly when an outbreak occurs.

Together, these metrics demonstrate that preventing disease entry is only one component of zoonotic disease mitigation. Domestic surveillance, outbreak control, producer participation and effective livestock traceability are also essential to protecting animal and human health.
limitations: The Indicator continues to provide a high-level picture and does not identify diseases, species, regions, investigation numbers or affected animals. The zero-entry measure is binary and does not capture intercepted shipments, near misses or threats mitigated before entry.

The outbreak rate includes animal diseases that may not be zoonotic and therefore cannot be interpreted as a direct measure of human-health risk. It is also influenced by surveillance intensity and specific events such as highly pathogenic avian influenza. The producer measure covers participants in six voluntary terrestrial animal-health programs and does not represent all Canadian producers. Changes may reflect enrolment rather than changes in on-farm biosecurity. Similarly, the traceability metric confirms that a national system exists but does not measure its coverage, data completeness, reporting timeliness, compliance or effectiveness during an outbreak. It does not cover all livestock species, and traceability requirements and delivery systems may vary by species and jurisdiction. Proposed amendments to strengthen livestock traceability requirements had not been finalized as of June 2026.1
The Indicator does not directly measure human zoonotic infections, wildlife reservoirs, occupational exposure or transmission among animals, people and the environment.
opportunities: Future reporting could present results by disease, species, region and zoonotic potential, while including surveillance coverage, investigations, affected premises and response times. Reporting interceptions and emerging international threats would provide a more complete assessment of border preparedness.

Producer measures could include program enrolment, vaccination, biosecurity-plan adoption and compliance outcomes. Linking CFIA animal-health data with human-health, wildlife and environmental surveillance would strengthen the One Health approach. Greater alignment with World Organisation for Animal Health, World Health Organization and FAO early-warning systems would improve comparability, preparedness and transparency.
notes: In June 2026, CFIA announced a revised regulatory approach that would advance updated traceability requirements for goats, sheep, cervids and pigs, while pausing proposed new movement-reporting requirements for cattle and bison. Final stakeholder engagement and publication in the Canada Gazette, Part II were still pending.

FI.5.title: Traceability Implementation
about: Traceability in the food system ensures that products can be tracked one step forward and one step back across the supply chain. It enables rapid responses to food-safety incidents, supports targeted recalls, protects public health, and contributes to transparency and consumer confidence.

The Indicator includes two metrics: Sector Coverage of Traceability Requirements, which outlines the food-system activities covered by Canadian regulations; and Number of Valid Safe Food for Canadians Licence Holders, which provides an indication of the scale of federally regulated food businesses. Both metrics relate to the Safe Food for Canadians Regulations, administered by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency for food imported, exported, or traded interprovincially.

The licence-holder metric adds important quantitative information to the Indicator. The previous metric described only the existence and scope of traceability requirements. The new measure helps show how many federally licensed businesses operate within the regulatory system, although it does not directly measure compliance or traceability performance.
observations: Under the Safe Food for Canadians Regulations, covered food businesses are generally required to maintain records that allow food to be traced forward to the immediate customer and back to the immediate supplier. Requirements apply to a broad range of activities, including importing, exporting, manufacturing, processing, treating, preserving, grading, packaging, labelling, and storing food for interprovincial or international trade.¹

Retail businesses—including supermarkets, farmers’ markets, grocery stores, bakeries, and butcher shops—must generally trace food back to their immediate supplier but are not required to identify individual consumers. Restaurants and similar enterprises are excluded from these retail traceability provisions.

Traceability documents must identify the food, usually through its common name and a lot code or other unique identifier. They must also record relevant transaction dates and the names and addresses of immediate suppliers and customers, as applicable. Businesses must be able to provide required traceability documents to CFIA within 24 hours of a request, or within a shorter period when CFIA considers the information necessary to address a risk of injury to human health.1

As of April 10, 2025, the Safe Food for Canadians Licence Registry listed 21,026 valid licence holders. This result demonstrates the broad regulatory reach of the federal licensing framework and provides an initial quantitative measure of the number of businesses operating within it.

However, the number of valid licence holders may change as licences are issued, renewed, amended, suspended, or cancelled. A licence may also cover multiple activities or establishments. The result should therefore not be interpreted as the number of distinct physical facilities or as evidence that all licence holders fully comply with traceability requirements.
limitations: The current metrics assess regulatory scope rather than implementation effectiveness. They do not show whether licence holders maintain complete and accurate records, how quickly products can be traced, or whether systems are interoperable across businesses and jurisdictions.

The licence registry does not represent every food business in Canada. Businesses operating solely within a province may be governed primarily by provincial requirements, while restaurants and certain direct-to-consumer activities are excluded from particular federal provisions. Small businesses may also experience greater financial, technical, and administrative barriers to adopting digital traceability systems.

There is no consistent national measure of traceability compliance, record completeness, recall response time, or the proportion of food that can be traced electronically from its origin through the supply chain. The number of licence holders therefore provides information on regulatory reach but not the quality, speed, or effectiveness of traceability implementation.
opportunities: Future reporting could measure compliance with record-keeping requirements, record completeness, response times, and the proportion of affected products successfully identified and removed during recalls. Results could be reported by commodity, activity, business size, and domestic or imported origin.

A national digital traceability framework could improve interoperability and information exchange while supporting small and medium-sized businesses with technology adoption. International developments also provide an opportunity for alignment. The United States’ FSMA 204 rule will require additional electronic traceability records for specified higher-risk foods, with enforcement not expected before July 20, 2028.2 Preparing Canadian exporters for these requirements could protect market access while strengthening domestic traceability capacity.
notes: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Regulatory requirements: Traceability for food
U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Food Traceability Final Rule

EC.1.title: National Economic Contribution
about: The National Economic Contribution indicator assesses the overall economic significance and contribution of Canada’s agriculture and agri-food sector to the national economy. This includes the agriculture, food, beverage and tobacco manufacturing, farm and food wholesale, retail and foodservice industries, as well as some farm input industries, such as pesticides, fertilizers and other agricultural chemicals, which were added to the Index this year.

This indicator describes the sector’s economic contribution to the national economy using data on gross domestic product (GDP), employment, and trade in absolute and relative terms. These indicators align with other indicators in the Economic block by emphasizing measurable economic outcomes and performance at the national level.
observations: Canada’s agriculture and agri-food (AAF) sector continues to grow, both in dollar terms and as a share of the overall economy. GDP of the sector’s players (agriculture, food, beverage and tobacco manufacturing (FBT), food wholesale, retail and food service and some inputs) rose to almost $150 billion in 2025 from $145 billion in 2024, up 2.5%. It accounted for the same share of the total economy as last year, at 6.5%.

Most of this growth in GDP was attributable to higher agriculture output, up 9.1% year on year to $38.3 billion, to account for the largest share of AAF sector GDP. This is the first time agriculture GDP has exceeded that of FBT manufacturing, which fell 2.8% to $36.5 billion in 2025. However, FBT manufacturing still accounts for the largest share of manufacturing GDP at 18.2% of the total, unchanged from 2024. GDP in food retailing and foodservices grew modestly, by 0.8% and 0.7% respectively, while that of food wholesaling was up 3 % and farm product wholesaling was up 7.8% over 2024. GDP of pesticides, fertilizers and other ag chemicals was down 12% in 2025.

Employment in the agriculture and agri-food (AAF) sector fell modestly in 2025 (-0.8%) to 2,299,587 from 2,317,421 a year earlier, despite the increase in sector output. Employment in all industries in the sector fell except for food manufacturing, which was up 0.6%. The agriculture and agri-food sector depends to a great extent on temporary and immigrant labour which due to the change in immigration policy in 2025, led to lower employment levels. At the same time, the number of indigenous individuals employed in agriculture, natural resources and utilities who do not live on reserves continues to increase to 45,100 in 2025, from 44,000 in 2024, up 2.5%, supported by concerted efforts to promote indigenous agriculture in Canada.

Canadian trade in agriculture and agri-food products has been impacted by geopolitical uncertainty and disruptive trade policies in the U.S. and elsewhere. Nevertheless, agriculture and agri-food (AAF) exports rose to $99.6 billion in 2025, up 0.7%. However, imports rose by more, to $74.7 billion so that the trade balance fell 11.9% to $25.2 billion in 2025. Yet as a share of total Canadian exports, the sector’s share remained unchanged at 12.8%. As a share of global trade, Canada’s AAF exports also fell to 2%.
limitations: This indicator measures the AAF sector’s significance and contribution to the Canadian economy at an aggregate level so does not provide information about individual farm and food businesses, or profitability at the firm level, or to reflect more detailed regional disparities. It also does not evaluate environmental or social trade-offs associated with economic growth which would help link economic to environmental indicators better.
opportunities: Most metrics included in this indicator are available from Statistics Canada on a regular basis, and have fairly high levels of confidence, given their importance for estimating Canadian economic activity. However, data for some of the industries included in the agri-food system measuring agri-business activity or farm inputs, are not as easily available. Given the role of rising costs of inputs and the changing nature of agri-businesses to include more agri-tech businesses, the indicator would benefit from better data for these sub-industries in determining the sector’s significance and contribution.

EC.2.title: Farm Financial Vibrancy & Resilience
about: The Financial Vibrancy & Resiliency indicator assesses the financial performance, stability, and long-term viability of Canada’s farming and agri-food sectors. It evaluates the sectors’ ability to generate income, attract investment, manage financial risk, and maintain resilience in the face of economic and market fluctuations. It also measures infrastructure and productive capacity, including both capital and labour gaps, and assesses the sector’s resilience and vulnerability to external shocks.

This indicator reflects how well the agri-food system is positioned to sustain operations, adapt to challenges, and support future growth by remaining competitive and resilient over time. It captures multiple dimensions of financial health, including profitability, debt-asset ratios and return on investment, capital stock, production capacity, labour gaps, and bankruptcy rates. It also includes metrics describing the state of Canada’s infrastructure that is important for sustaining trade and sector performance, through broadband coverage and rail and greenhouse assets. Supply chain resilience captures the vulnerability of the sector to trade and domestic shocks through its measures of import and export dependency.
observations: Financial metrics for the farm and food and beverage manufacturing sectors reveal how the sector was under pressure in 2025 yet still managed to remain profitable. Net farm cash income (NCI) rose by 2.7% in 2025, as revenues rose more than expenses. However, compared to its five- year average, NCI was down 5.8%. Despite lower program payments, market receipts rose 6.1% as revenues were boosted by stronger commodity prices, particularly for livestock. The debt-to-asset ratio on the average farm stabilized around 0.16, yet farm bankruptcies for crop farmers rose in 2025 to .0017. The percentage of financially healthy farms declined slightly to 91% in 2024/25 from 92% in 2022/23. Bankruptcy rates in most other agri-food industries fell, reflecting improved financial performance, while those in beverage and tobacco businesses rose from .0067 in 2023 to .0173 in 2025, due to restructuring in cannabis production due to regulatory changes and market conditions.

In food manufacturing, profitability was up as revenues rose more than expenses and the industry’s return on equity (ROE) increased to 9.6% in 2024, up from 8.5% in 2023. Beverage manufacturing saw its ROE rise as well to 6.6% from 5.7%. Both industries saw reduced capacity utilization and lower capital investments in 2025, with investment in food manufacturing falling to $ 7.9 billion from $8.2 billion in 2024.

Job vacancies were down in food and beverage manufacturing in 2025 to 2.3% and 2.6% respectively. Other agri-food industries also experienced a decline in job vacancies, including retail (4.5%) and restaurants (4.5%) as labour market conditions strengthened.

To facilitate production and export marketing capacity in the agri-food sector, adequate infrastructure is important. In 2025, broadband coverage improved, rising to 97.3% nationally and 86.9% in rural Canada. It also rose to 71.8% coverage for First Nations. The number of rail cars unloaded at Western ports, from where a significant portion of Canada’s agriculture products are shipped, rose from 36,528 to 51,849 as Canada boosted exports in 2025. Greenhouse area expanded to reach 35.9 billion square metres under glass, up1.4% over the previous year as the greenhouse industry continued to experience significant expansion.

The sector’s resilience is determined to a great degree by its reliance on the share of production that is exported, and on the degree to which Canada relies on imports for both its intermediate inputs and finished food products. New metrics added to Index 2.0 this year measure these. In 2024, food, beverage and tobacco manufacturing reduced their dependence on imports, with imports falling as a share of domestic availability from -% to -% in food manufacturing. Pesticides and agricultural implements industries boosted theirs. In terms of export market concentration, food manufacturing was able to reduce its dependence on exporting while beverage and tobacco manufacturing increased theirs.

Other metrics were added this year to measure resilience at the farm level. Metrics measuring the average age of farmers and the share of farms that report having succession plans for farm transitioning are being proposed to reflect how resilient and adaptable farmers are and how probable they will remain so in the future. These metrics, which show how producers are aging and the low rate of succession planning, measure the extent to which there is a risk that there will be fewer farmers in the future. The average age of farmers continues to rise, to 56 years old (in 2021), and the share of farms with a succession plan how the transfer of farm assets to a new generation may run into difficulties, are important for describing the resilience of the sector.
limitations: Being able to measure profitability and resilience at the farm and firm level for this sector is less reliable because of the lower frequency of farm financial survey data being collected (every two years) or due to the lag in balance sheet data from industry financial statements. Hence the picture provided here currently is somewhat dated and less up to date. Also, only industry averages are available, which can mask large differences among individual farm and firm players.
opportunities: Resilience is clearly a characteristic of the sector that is needed in these times of uncertainty and geopolitical turmoil, allowing the industry to bounce back from shocks and adapt. Apart from the metrics that have recently been introduced, there are likely opportunities to find additional measures of resilience in the sector. Administrative data, which are available from farm programs may provide new opportunities to find metrics that tell of the financial viability of the sector, something that Statistics Canada has been increasingly open to do.

EC.3.title: Innovation
about: The Innovation indicator provides measures of innovation which cover various aspects of the innovation continuum. This includes public and private investments in research, extension, commercialization, and adoption of new technologies, products, processes and marketing and management practices at both the farm and food and beverage manufacturing level. This indicator also includes measures of regulatory compliance and burden that impact and often impede the extent to which new products and processes can be developed, commercialized and adopted.

The indicator assesses the capacity of Canada’s agri-food sector to develop, adopt, and scale innovations that enhance productivity, sustainability, and competitiveness. It evaluates research and development (R&D) activity, regulatory processes that enable innovation, and the extent to which new technologies and practices are adopted by both producers and food and beverage manufacturers.

The indicator captures how innovation supports improvements in production efficiency, environmental performance, and value creation across the agri-food system. It considers both public and private investment in innovation, as well as the ecosystem that facilitates the development and commercialization of new solutions. This indicator aligns with the Economic block through its focus on long-term growth, competitiveness, and system transformation.
observations: According to the OECD, government expenditures on R&D in agriculture have grown over the past five years after having declined in the previous decade. These expenditures rose 0.5% to $990.5 million in 2024 from $985.4 million in 2023 as spending on knowledge transfer increased while that of knowledge generation (i.e. R&D) remained flat. The government’s focus on climate change meant that much of the R&D spending was focused on GHG emissions reductions rather than productivity enhancing innovations. Private sector investment in in-house R&D by food and beverage manufacturing declined in 2024 after having increased to decade high levels in 2023. Private sector R&D in agriculture was also down in 2025 from peaks in 2020.

Along the innovation continuum, adoption of new technologies, products, processes or business practices are important metrics of innovation. At the farm level, data from the Farm Management Survey showed how 84% of crop farmers adopted GPS technology in 2021, unchanged from this rate in 2016. Other farm practices that were being readily adopted include automation, robotic milking and precision agriculture. For food and beverage manufacturers, the most recent survey of innovation in food processing showed that 67.7% of food manufacturing businesses had introduced at least one innovation between 2021 and 2023, but this was down from 72.1% between 2016 and 2018, the last year of the survey. Process innovations declined the most, and larger businesses were more likely to innovate than smaller businesses.

Innovation and growth is known to be impacted by regulatory burden. This is because compliance becomes costly as it delays production and slows approvals of new products. In this way regulations impact the efficiency with which agriculture and food products can be produced and marketed in Canada. An increase in regulatory burden makes Canada’s agriculture and agri-food industry less competitive with impacts on costs and prices for consumers. In 2025, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), which is responsible for regulations covering plant and animal health and disease, food safety, inspection of licensed establishments, labelling and packaging and trade regulations, saw the number of regulatory requirements increase from 4,395 in 2025, up 5% from 4,178 in 2024. However, compared to the 2014 baseline count, the number was down 60%.

Another metric which reflects the impact of regulations on the sector is that related to the speed of approvals of pest control products. In 2022/23, 91% of Category B submissions to the Pest Management Review Agency which approves pest products were completed within the established service standards or negotiated timelines, and this was down slightly from 92% in 2022/22.
limitations: Similar to other indicators, there are limitations in finding regular and easily accessible data to describe innovation in the sector. Many of metrics rely on surveys that are only collected every two years or sporadically. And even if the data is available, it often comes at a cost or is difficult to find.
opportunities: Innovation is a key predictor of future productivity and economic growth and competitiveness, with the introduction and adoption of new technologies and new products that meet consumer demand. Being able to find new data and indicators of innovation will help us understand better the prospects for future growth and competitiveness of the agriculture and agrifood sector. Better data on regulatory compliance and burden would provide us with a better sense of where the barriers to economic growth and innovation are.

EC.4.title: Sustainable Finance
about: The Sustainable Finance indicator assesses the extent to which financial resources are mobilized to support sustainability objectives within Canada’s agri-food sector. It evaluates both market-based and public funding mechanisms that enable investments in climate-smart practices, environmental improvements, and broader sustainability outcomes across the value chain.

The indicator captures financial flows directed toward sustainability, including private capital, investments aligned with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria, and government or NGO funding programs that promote climate smart agriculture. It reflects how financial systems are evolving to support the transition toward more sustainable agri-food production and supply chains.
observations: In 2025, a change in policies in Ottawa led to more focus on growth and competitiveness by the new Carney government. One of agriculture’s key funding programs, the Living Labs was terminated. However, federal government funding to support the On-Farm Climate Action Fund under the Agriculture Climate Solutions program rose to $108.6 million in 2024/25, from $96.1 million in 2022/23. The program first launched in Budget 2021, was to allocate $704.1 million to this program over a five-year period, and additional funds were added to support Eastern farmers facing high fertilizer costs in 2022. Other sustainability funding programs related to Clean technology continued to be funded in Budget 2025.
limitations: This indicator aligns with the Economic block by focusing on the financial foundations that enable sustainable transformation, but it does not assess the effectiveness of individual investments or quantify sustainability impacts directly but rather emphasizes the availability and direction of capital toward sustainability goals. More metrics could be developed to measure this aspect of financial support. The current metrics which reflect federal government funding of climate smart agriculture programs at AAFC may have to be updated because some of the programming under this category is being discontinued.
opportunities: Sustainable finance has evolved as an area to cover financing initiatives that incent environmental practices to mitigate and adapt to climate change, and also to help companies report on ESG results and support from financial institutions. More recent developments in sustainable finance are identifying ways to mobilize investments to support nature and nature-based solutions and assets. Hence future versions of the Index may develop more metrics along these lines.

EC.5.title: Productivity
about: The productivity indicator is a new addition to Index 2.0 this year. It is important because of its direct link to economic growth, competitiveness and sustainability. It measures the industry’s ability to produce more and better with less. Productivity is measured by comparing the output that is produced with a given amount of inputs, such as labour, capital, land or raw materials. Productivity growth occurs when more output is produced with the same amount of inputs, or when the same amount of output can be produced with fewer inputs. This ensures the sector remains sustainable and can lead to lower costs and greater profitability as well as increased competitiveness and economic growth.

The most common productivity metric is labour productivity which measures output from a given amount of labour, such as output per employee or per hour worked. Labour productivity is provided for the agriculture, and food and beverage manufacturing industry. Other partial productivity metrics are available but are less often reported, such as capital productivity. However, crop yields measured as bushels per hectare are another important partial productivity metric included in Index 2.0. But partial productivity metrics only tell part of the story. This is told by Total Factor productivity or Multifactor productivity which are provided for agriculture and for food and beverage manufacturing respectively. These account for how efficiently all inputs are combined to produce the sector’s output. These total (multi) productivity metrics reflect the impact of new technologies, or even new ways of managing or organizing production that lead to greater efficiency and possibly even scale.
observations: One of the new metrics introduced in Version 2.0 of the Index is labour productivity in agriculture and food and beverage manufacturing, which measure output per hours worked. Over the period 2011 to 2025, labour productivity in food manufacturing grew 0.7% per year, from $53.70 per hour to $59.10 per hour. It grew faster (1.4%) in the earlier part of the period (2011 to 2018) than in the latter part (2019 to 2025), when it hardly grew, reflecting a slowdown in productivity in the Canadian economy more broadly. This was true for all industries, from agriculture (2.6%) to total manufacturing (-1.5%) to beverage and tobacco manufacturing (-4.7%). The significant productivity slowdown after 2019 may be partly explained by COVID in 2020-22 which disrupted labour markets, but it could also reflect a more significant structural change, due to inflation, higher costs and commodity prices or reduced business investments after 2019.

Total factor productivity (TFP) in agriculture is another new metric introduced this year. This metric is produced by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) based on a collaboration of international experts who provide individual country data and expertise from Canada and other countries. Similar to MFP, these data tell us that between 1991 and 2000, productivity growth grew by 2.1% per year, leading to agricultural output growth of 2.3% per year as inputs grew only marginally. Over the more recent period, 2020 to 2023, Canada experienced a large decline in agricultural output (-1.7%) primarily due to negative productivity growth (-1.1%%) as a result of a major drought on the Prairies in 2021 which reduced agricultural production dramatically.
limitations: This indicator aligns with the Economic block by focusing on efficiency, competitiveness, and long-term economic performance of the agri-food system. It does not measure profitability at the firm level, nor does it directly assess environmental or social outcomes, although productivity improvements may have implications for both.
opportunities: There is a possibility to improve the productivity indicators by drawing on other sources of data and analysis that can help explain and reinforce the significance of this indicator for telling the story about economic sustainability. Other sources include the OECD, the Bank of Canada and the Canadian Centre for the Study of Living Standards that put significant resources into the development of data and analysis explaining productivity metrics.

SW.1.title: Decent Work for People
about: Decent Work for People refers to the extent to which Canada’s agri-food sector provides opportunities for women and men to obtain productive work in conditions of freedom, equity, security and human dignity and contributing to the social sustainability of the agri-food system.
The indicator also examines how labour conditions contribute to the long-term social sustainability, resilience, and attractiveness of the agri-food sector.

New metrics have been added to provide more accurate and comprehensive information and to better align the Indicator with the International Labour Organization’s Decent Work Agenda. Together, these metrics assess whether the sector offers stable, equitable, and rewarding work environments for current and future generations.
observations: Mental health remains a concern for farmers. The average perceived-stress score was 18.72 out of 40 in 2021, close to 18.9 in 2015–16. In the 2021 survey, 26.8% of farmers screened positive for anxiety and 23.6% screened positive for major depressive disorder. These are screening results, not clinical diagnoses. During the COVID-19 pandemic, 20.9% reported using resources to manage emotional, mental-health or substance-use concerns. Farm-related fatalities numbered 48 in 2020, compared with 91 in 2010, although annual totals fluctuated. Succession planning was also limited: in 2021, 12% of agricultural operations had a written plan, while 66.1% had not discussed succession.

Measures of inclusion show persistent gaps. Women made up 46.2% of the agri-food workforce in 2025 and 30.4% of farm operators in 2021, but held 15% of seats on the sector association boards reviewed in 2025. In 2025, women’s average hourly wages were 88% of men’s, and their average weekly wages were 79.4% of men’s. Indigenous employment in the broader agriculture, natural resources and utilities category rose from 43,300 in 2023 to 45,100 in 2025.
