The workbook also records 1,355 employers publicly listed as non-compliant under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program from June 2016 to July 2026. Because this is a cumulative count, it should not be interpreted as an annual non-compliance rate.

Measures of workforce renewal point in different directions. Enrolment in agriculture and related postsecondary fields rose from 11,445 in 2016/17 to 19,833 in 2023/24, and 4-H Canada reported 19,694 members in 2025–26. Meanwhile, the share of agri-food workers aged 15–24 fell from 27.8% in 2023 to 25.1% in 2025. Workers aged 55 and over accounted for 19.2% of the workforce in 2025. These measures show participation in education and youth programs alongside workforce trends; they do not establish how many participants subsequently enter agri-food employment.

New measures add detail on job opportunities and worker representation. In 2024, job vacancy rates ranged from 2.5% in food manufacturing to 4.9% in food services and drinking places. Average weekly earnings in food manufacturing reached $1,249.75 in 2025. The workbook reports unionization rates of 3% in agriculture, 21.6% in manufacturing and 5.9% in accommodation and food services. These industry figures provide useful context, but their categories do not all match the combined agri-food workforce used in the other measures.
limitations: The main challenge is that the available measures do not form a consistent picture of decent work over time or across the whole agri-food system. Several come from infrequent or one-off surveys. Even where earlier results exist, comparisons can be difficult: the farmer mental-health studies, for example, used different screening tools. Industry coverage also varies. Some datasets group agriculture with natural resources and utilities, while others report on manufacturing or services more broadly, making it difficult to isolate food processing, retail and food service.

These gaps also limit how closely the indicator can reflect the ILO Decent Work Agenda. The new unionization measure offers a starting point for understanding worker representation, but it does not show the full extent of collective bargaining coverage or how labour rights are exercised in practice. Employment security, working hours, social protection and access to workplace complaint mechanisms likewise cannot yet be assessed consistently across the sector.
opportunities: Recent initiatives connect directly to the Decent Work for People metrics. Federal funding for farm safety could support progress on workplace fatalities and farmer mental health, while the Youth Employment and Skills Program offers paid experience at a time when the share of young agri-food workers is declining.1 Annual Temporary Foreign Worker Program inspection results could also add context to the Index’s cumulative count of non-compliant employers.2

The Centre’s work to align this indicator with the ILO Decent Work Agenda is an opportunity to identify gaps in the current metrics and develop a more complete picture of employment conditions, worker protections and social dialogue across the agri-food system..

SW.2.title: Food Security
about: Food security reflects whether all individuals have consistent physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food. It is a cornerstone of a sustainable food system and depends on more than food supply alone. In the National Index, Food Security refers to the extent to which individuals and households in Canada have consistent and reliable access to sufficient, safe, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food, enabled by a food system that makes food affordable, accessible, and stable over time.

New metrics have been added to provide more accurate and comprehensive information and to better align the Indicator with the Food and Agriculture Organization’s food security framework. Metrics are drawn primarily from Statistics Canada, Food Banks Canada, the OECD, the FAO and World Bank, and Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada.
observations: Food insecurity rose sharply between 2021 and 2023, then eased slightly in 2024. The share of people living in households experiencing marginal, moderate or severe food insecurity increased from 18.5% in 2021 to 25.7% in 2023, before falling to 24.0% in 2024. Even after that decline, the rate remained 5.5 percentage points above its 2021 level. Including marginal food insecurity captures households facing uncertainty about access to food, as well as those experiencing more severe difficulties.

The burden remained uneven in 2024. Food insecurity affected 34.7% of First Nations, Métis and Inuit people, 30.8% of children and 30.4% of people in visible minority groups, compared with 11.9% of seniors. The rates for women and men were closer, at 24.2% and 23.9%, respectively.

Food costs continued to rise over the same period. The Consumer Price Index for food reached 195.3 in 2025, up from 189.3 in 2024 and 171.5 in 2022, with 2002 set at 100. The estimated cost of a healthy diet also increased from 4.8 purchasing power parity dollars per person per day in 2023 to 5.5 in 2025. For households in the lowest-income quintile, the workbook reports food spending equivalent to 27.7% of income in 2025, while food accounted for 9.5% of total household expenditures across all households in 2024. These percentages use different denominators and cannot be compared directly.

Demand for food assistance remained high. Canadian food banks recorded 2,165,776 visits in 2025, approximately 5.2% more than in 2024 and 11.9% more than in 2023. Nutrition North Canada expenditures rose from $131.3 million in 2022–23 to $185.8 million in 2024–25. The workbook also estimates $203.3 million for 2025–26, but identifies that figure as provisional pending published actual expenditures.
limitations: Current household measures focus primarily on food insecurity resulting from financial constraints. They do not fully address other aspects of food security, including availability, physical access, utilization, stability, quality, and cultural acceptability.

The household series currently used ends in 2023, while the other metrics cover different periods and populations. Food-bank visits represent instances of service use rather than unique individuals, and program expenditures do not demonstrate whether affordability or access has improved.

Challenges were also encountered in identifying credible, regularly updated, and nationally comparable data for all dimensions of the FAO framework. Canada’s National Food Security Strategy includes targets related mainly to domestic production, processing capacity, and import dependence, but provides limited measures for tracking household food insecurity and unequal access to nutritious food1.
opportunities: Future reporting should incorporate the latest household results and track marginal, moderate, and severe food insecurity separately. More detailed reporting by province, territory, Indigenous identity, age, and income would provide a clearer picture of unequal outcomes.

The National Food Security Strategy creates an opportunity to connect the Indicator with national priorities for affordability, domestic production, supply-chain resilience, and northern access. Future reporting could assess whether its initiatives lead to measurable improvements in household food insecurity, healthy-food affordability, and access among vulnerable populations. Integrating food security with income, housing, transportation, and geographic isolation would further strengthen the Indicator and its alignment with the FAO framework.
notes: Launched by the Government of Canada in 2026, the National Food Security Strategy aims to make food more affordable and accessible while strengthening domestic food production, processing capacity, supply chains, and resilience to international disruptions. Its initiatives seek to increase competition, expand food-processing infrastructure, support year-round production, reduce dependence on imports, and improve access to fresh food in rural, remote, and northern communities. Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, National Food Security Strategy, 2026.

SW.3.title: Animal Care
about: Animal care standards are central to ethical and sustainable food systems. In Canada, these standards are established through species-specific Codes of Practice developed by the National Farm Animal Care Council in collaboration with industry, government, animal-welfare organizations, researchers, and veterinary experts. This Indicator is divided into two components: Farm Animal Care and Welfare Standards, which examines the national framework, Codes of Practice, audit systems, and livestock traceability; and On-Farm Animal Care and Welfare Practices, which assesses selected practices for dairy cattle, laying hens, and beef cattle.

New metrics have been added to provide more accurate and comprehensive information on how national standards are assessed and applied. This responds to limitations identified in the 2025 Index, which focused primarily on whether Codes of Practice existed.
observations: Canada has maintained a national farm animal care framework since 2005. Codes of Practice are periodically reviewed and updated to reflect evolving science, production practices, and public expectations. Recent activity includes updates for dairy cattle in 2023, pigs in 2024, and pullets and laying hens in 2025. Codes for beef cattle, pigs, sheep, poultry, and equine are currently under revision.1

Eight of the 14 animal industries covered by the national framework have an NFACC-recognized animal-care assessment or audit program. This new metric addresses a gap identified in 2025 by showing whether industries have established systems for assessing the implementation of their Codes. However, it does not yet show the proportion of farms participating or the results of assessments.

The new on-farm metrics provide an initial picture of selected animal-care practices. A 2023 dairy study found that 75% of surveyed farms provided outdoor access to at least one class of cattle. Access varied from 29% for lactating cows and 27% for young heifers to 48% for dry cows and pregnant heifers.2

Laying-hen housing systems also varied. In 2024, 43% of hens were housed in conventional systems and 37% in enriched systems. Free-run systems accounted for 13.5%, organic systems for 4.9%, and free-range systems for 1.4%.

Among surveyed beef producers, 97% reported training handlers in low-stress animal-handling practices, 88% had taken measures to support cattle during extreme weather events, and 81% had a veterinarian-client-patient relationship. These results suggest high reported adoption of selected practices supporting cattle health and welfare.
limitations: Public reporting remains limited on the adoption, implementation, and effectiveness of Codes of Practice. The existence of an audit system does not show how many farms are assessed, the level of compliance achieved, or whether corrective actions are completed.

On-farm metrics cover only selected species and practices. Dairy and beef results are based on surveys or one-off studies and may not represent all Canadian farms. Self-reported practices also do not confirm consistent implementation. Outdoor access and housing systems describe production conditions but do not independently demonstrate animal-welfare outcomes.

Credible, nationally comparable data remain limited for mortality, injury, lameness, disease, pain management, transport losses, and emergency preparedness. Differences in species, production systems, and provincial requirements also make consistent national comparisons difficult.
opportunities: Future reporting could track participation in recognized assessment programs, audit results, non-compliance findings, and corrective actions. Publicly available uptake statistics would improve transparency and show how consistently standards are applied.

Integrating animal-based outcomes—including mortality, injury, lameness, disease incidence, body condition, and transport losses—would help determine whether standards and practices lead to better welfare. Recurring data by species, region, and production system would improve comparability. Aligning the Indicator with World Organisation for Animal Health standards and international benchmarking tools would further strengthen accountability and demonstrate leadership in animal care.
